processing: Made as part of the Yamato-cha range, typically as steamed sencha.
harvest_season: Little is documented for Tsukigase alone; as with other Japanese green teas, the spring first flush is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Fine dark green needles, as is typical of sencha.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green, as is typical of sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft mid-green leaf, as is typical of steamed tea.
taste_profile: Few notes exist for Tsukigase alone. Yamato highland tea generally is fragrant, with a sweet, savoury depth.

brewing.notes: Typical settings for sencha. Native-seed teas from here deserve a cooler first steep so you can taste how they differ.

vintage_note: Usual for Japanese green tea: sold as the current year's harvest, with spring first flush at the top, and best drunk within about a year. It may be sold as Tsukigase-cha or under the wider Yamato-cha name, so the label does not always show the sub-area.
description:
Tsukigase-cha is one of the place names inside Yamato-cha, from the Tsukigase district in the northeast of Nara, better known to many Japanese for its plum groves. Green tea labelling standards let it appear under its own name or under the general one.

It shares the conditions of the Yamato Highlands: cool, misty, big swings between day and night. Growers credit these for the sweetness in their leaf. Most tea here follows the steamed sencha route, as is typical of the highlands.

Brew it as you would any good sencha and look for fragrance and soft sweetness. Little has been written about how Tsukigase differs from its neighbours, so comparing it with a tea from nearby Yagyu or Fukusumi is more useful than any guide.

The interesting find is sencha from native seed-grown bushes, zairai, which at least one specialist seller offers and describes as unlike the usual Japanese green. Otherwise, buy by farm and harvest date.
history:
Tsukigase's tea is documented mainly as part of the wider Yamato-cha story, and its own beginnings are little recorded.

The recent name to know is Kamikubo Tea Garden, whose grower won the agriculture minister's award at the 25th national hand-rolled tea competition and received the title of chasei, reportedly the first in the Kansai region.
